Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: What are some sayings in English that seem strange to non-native speakers?
Answer: When I lived in Nottingham, there was a famous exclamation people sometimes quoted to me, in somewhat conspiratorial spirits, it would seem: “Ay up me duck!” When I first heard it, on a tram, I thought the person saying it wanted me to relinquish my seat to him. I did wonder why he referred to me as a duck, but… when in Rome. And I lived in Nottingham for many years without anyone ever explaining what that saying means. And maybe there is no known explanation for it. But then I came to Stockholm and started using the underground system. That’s where I believe to have found a possible origin for “Ay up me duck” - in the Swedish language, possibly hinting at a Norse connection. As you approach the escalators in the Stockholm metro, coming from a train, those escalators coming down are signposted as “Ej Upp” - literally not up. You see it on the left side in the picture: That’s when it dawned on me that “Ay up” could be the same as “ej upp”, which would then interpret the meaning of “Ay up me duck” to be something like “don’t fly away, my duck!” I’d like that. Very sweet, like saying “don’t go away now, sweetie”. I could see that very much in line with the warm, jovial character of northern England.

Name: Chris Ebbert
Question: Do you think the Lincoln Town Car should have been discontinued?
Answer: I believe Ford has missed an opportunity when they discontinued the Town Car. Perhaps they didn’t see the connection when it happened in 2011, but if they had waited a bit, the Town Car with its ladder frame and high payload capability would have been a brilliant electric livery and limousine service vehicle. Just like the electric F-150, it could have carried enough batteries to ensure a long range, and it would then have been one supremely smooth and quiet work horse for all the companies that have been banking on that model for decades. Personally, I hope to electrify my Town Car some day. It will embody the Town Car values even more by being electric.

Question: How do you keep your car windows from freezing overnight?
Answer: It’s actually surprisingly easy to keep your car windows from freezing. Frost is simply ice crystals accumulating on a surface, so put something on your windscreen in ways that it won’t blow away over night, and you’re all set. Some people jam a piece of cardboard under their wipers, but I have something better. It’s a piece of neoprene foam matting, not the cheapest kind maybe - about 0.8 cm thick, and I think the piece I have there is worth about 20 USD. I’ve put duct tape across it, with wine corks at the end. The wine corks dangle inside the car when I close the doors, and the neoprene foam shield covers everything, including the wipers. You need the wine corks so the duct tape doesn’t get pulled out. We get winds of about 50 km/h, and they can’t think of anything more fun than to rip some 20 dollar piece of neoprene off a Toyota and carry it all the way to Norway. Some people try it with these aluminium thingies originally intended to cover the dash boards of parked cars in Portugal or Brazil. Me, too. These things last about three days when the weather is clement where I live. Then, it’s tinsel. (the cable is for the block heater, by the way, and it also feeds the interior fan heater that’s on a timer to bring the car’s interior from minus 35 Celsius to a balmy ten or so before the trip starts). As for the cardboard solution, it’s great until you put your ice encrusted piece of cardboard inside the car to go home. Once you get there, it’s porridge. Where I live, frost is not just frost. This is some spiky stuff. Walk on it, and it sounds like breaking glass. Forget about cardboard or aluminium foil. Floor mats is what you’ll want. And duct tape, and wine corks. You’ll need four wine corks, by the way. Start the project by buying four nice bottles of good, Argentinian red.
